The passive voice is used when the focus is on the action itself or the recipient of the action, rather than who performed it. It is often formed with a form of 'to be' (e.g., “is”, “are”, “was”, “were”) followed by the past participle of the main verb. This construction is common in news reporting, especially when the person or group doing the action is less important or obvious.

We use the passive voice when the action: We use the passive voice when the action is more important than the person or thing doing it, or when we don't know or don't want to say who performed the action. It is formed with a form of 'to be' (e.g., “is”, “are”, “was”, “were”) plus the past participle of the main verb. This construction shifts the focus from the doer to the receiver of the action.

We use the simple present tense to talk: We use the simple present tense to talk about facts or things that are generally true. The verb form stays the same for 'I', 'you', 'we', 'they', but we add “-s” or “-es” for 'he', 'she', or 'it'.
